title: Geodiversity

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit in 1992 not only brought a new word – biodiversity – into general use but also stimulated an international movement to conserve genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity. But it's wrong to equate nature conservation solely with wildlife conservation. Biodiversity is only half of the natural environment; the physical, inanimate world also has diversity, both in its geology (rocks, minerals, fossils), and geomorphology (landforms, processes). Geodiversity could be described as ‘the natural range of geological, geomorphological, and soil features’. Mick Stanley of environmental consultancy Geodiversity Consulting prefers a wider interpretation: ‘Geodiversity is the link between people, landscapes, and culture; it is the variety of geological environments, phenomena, and processes that make those landscapes, rocks, minerals, fossils, and soils that provide the framework for life on Earth.’

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: This latter point is worth noting because, without the variation in topography, physical processes, and geological materials, there would be much less biodiversity. But the world’s geodiversity is valuable for numerous other reasons, too. For example, almost all natural resources that aren't grown are derived from the Earth’s crust. Over the centuries, humans have exploited the diversity of these resources, whether it be metals, building materials, industrial minerals, gemstones, or fuels. Variations in topography are reflected by the diverse landscapes that provide the basis for many leisure activities, from skiing to tourism. Many geomorphological features around the world, such as Uluru (Ayers Rock) in Australia, also have spiritual value. And of course, the world’s geological resources have immense value to scientific research, with rock and fossil records providing the evidence to reconstruct the history of the Earth and the evolution of life.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is a natural tendency to think of wildlife as being fragile and vulnerable and therefore in need of conservation, whereas rocks and mountains tend to be seen as static and much too abundant ever to be endangered. This is an oversimplification because many geological sites are extremely fragile. In Carlsbad Caverns in New Mexico, USA, visitors have damaged thousands of valuable geological deposits in the area’s caves, often in seeking souvenirs of their visits. In north-western USA’s Yellowstone National Park, visitors have removed from the site a whole trunk of a tree composed of fossilized wood. At Crackington Haven in England, there is a renowned beach comprising dark grey rounded pebbles with attractive quartz veins, and a significant amount of this material has been removed to use in landscaping schemes. In Australia, the wholesale removal of exfoliated sandstone slabs from escarpments around Sydney for use in landscaping has been a major factor in the serious decline of a local snake species. Other risks to geodiversity include the quarrying of important landform features; urban expansion or hard engineering on the banks of rivers or on coastlines, thus destroying important geological sites; soil erosion resulting from unsustainable agricultural practices; and the remodelling of topography to create golf courses.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: But the biggest danger of all is probably ignorance of the potential impacts of human activity. When it comes to biodiversity, it may be possible to reintroduce species or establish seed or DNA banks, and in some cases, restoration of physical systems is also possible – for example, channelled rivers or coastlines obscured by hard sea However, this is not the case with all aspects of geodiversity. Once destroyed, important rock, mineral, and fossil sites aren't restorable, and this means that their conservation is even more important.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is, however, a growing awareness of the importance of protecting precious geodiversity sites, and there is a hierarchy of measures available, from the international to the local level. For instance, there are more than 100 World Heritage sites of geological interest. Some, such as the Grand Canyon, Canadian Rocky Mountains, Galápagos Islands, and Great Barrier Reef, are world-famous, but others are barely known. One such is Miguasha National Park in south-east Quebec, Canada, which is the world’s most outstanding site for fossil fish of the Devonian period, a key geological era around 400 million years ago. A more recent UNESCO-supported programme is the Global Geoparks initiative, which currently comprises 54 geoparks – 32 sites in Europe, 18 in China, and one each in Brazil, Iran, Australia, and Malaysia. Geoparks are areas where the significant geological heritage is used to promote sustainable geotourism, thus benefiting the local economy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In recent years, conservationists have come to realise that using protected areas to safeguard specific sites often results in a fragmented network that is vulnerable to widespread threats such as climate change or other forces at work outside the area’s boundaries: there’s little point in protecting a lake if the rivers that empty into it are highly polluted. It is therefore important to implement what could be termed ‘wider landscape’ techniques. Biodiversity conservation is partially fulfilling this role by protecting habitats as well as species. But what of geodiversity? Ideally, the natural topography and physical processes should be protected and restored, particularly where changes are made. For example, where topography is to be remodelled in golf course construction, it should respect the character of the natural landforms. With government planning guidance in many countries now emphasising the importance of both biodiversity and geological conservation, it looks as though the neglect of the latter is being brought to an end, through an understanding that nature has geodiversity as well as biodiversity.

subtitle: To most people, conservation means preserving the world’s biodiversity: its animals and plants. But the physical Earth – rock, soil, fossils, minerals, and landforms – has its own values and threats
